sourceRecords.sermonTitle: The Impact of the Gospel In Relationships Pt. 11

entries.title: Romans: The Gospel and the Life It Produces
entries.commentary: Romans gives us a sustained explanation of the Gospel and God's saving work. We begin with the power of the Gospel and our universal problem of sin; we move through justification by faith, union with Christ, assurance in God's love, and God's purposes for Israel. That matters when we reach Romans 12. We do not obey its commands to purchase salvation. Because we have received God's mercy, our lives ought to reflect it, including the way we respond to people who wrong us. See Romans 1:16; 3:10; 4:1–3; 5:1–2; 6:1–4; 8:38–39; and 12:1–2.

entries.title: Romans 1: The Gospel Is God’s Power
entries.commentary: Romans 1:16 puts the Gospel's saving power at the beginning of Paul's message. The Gospel is not simply advice to become better people; it is God's message of salvation. When we later come to changed behavior in Romans 12, we must remember where that change begins.

entries.title: Romans 2: God Judges Impartially
entries.commentary: Romans 2 reminds us that God judges impartially. Jew and Gentile stand accountable before the same righteous Judge, and neither our religious standing nor our group identity removes our need for the Gospel. This is a chapter-level orientation, not an explanation of every judgment passage.

entries.title: Romans 3: The Universal Need of Grace
entries.commentary: Romans 3:10 brings us face to face with the universal problem of sin: none of us possesses righteousness that could establish our standing before God. That is why salvation rests on God's grace instead of our moral achievements.

entries.title: Romans 4: Abraham and Justification by Faith
entries.commentary: In Romans 4:1–3, Abraham shows us what justification by faith means. We do not earn a righteous standing with God through meritorious works. Keep that distinction in view when Paul later tells believers how they ought to live in Romans 12.

entries.title: Romans 5: Peace and Access Through Faith
entries.commentary: Romans 5:1–2 tells us what follows justification by faith: we have peace with God and access into grace through Jesus Christ. Our obedience grows out of that reconciled relationship; it does not purchase it.

entries.title: Romans 6: Newness of Life
entries.commentary: Romans 6 answers the mistaken idea that grace gives us permission to continue in sin. In Romans 6:1–4 we are identified with Christ in His death and resurrection, so newness of life follows salvation. That new life is the fruit of grace, never a substitute for grace.

entries.title: Romans 7: Belonging to the Risen Christ
entries.commentary: Romans 7:4 reminds us that we belong to the risen Christ and are to bear fruit for God. Our relationship to Christ is the foundation for faithful service. We do not obtain spiritual life through legal observance and then add Christ to it.

entries.title: Romans 8: Providence and Assurance
entries.commentary: Romans 8 gives us extraordinary confidence in God's care and saving love. Romans 8:28 speaks of His providential work; Romans 8:31 asks what can finally stand against those for whom God is working; and Romans 8:38–39 assures us that nothing can separate us from His love in Christ. That assurance is part of the mercy that ought to change the way we treat people.

entries.title: Romans 9–11: God’s Purposes and Wisdom
entries.commentary: Romans 9–11 brings us to weighty questions about election, predestination, and God's purposes for Israel. We cannot settle every disputed detail in a brief overview. But Paul's response in Romans 11:33–36 teaches us something essential: God's judgments and ways should lead us toward humility and worship.

entries.title: Romans 10:9–13: The Gospel Invitation
entries.commentary: Romans 10:9–13 gives us a precious Gospel invitation. We are called to confess Jesus as Lord and believe that God raised Him from the dead. The promise of salvation belongs within Paul's larger explanation of God's mercy, not within a plan for earning His favor.

entries.title: Romans 12: Mercy Expressed in a Changed Life
entries.commentary: Romans 12 turns the mercy Paul has explained into a call for a changed life. When we present ourselves to God and seek renewal of mind, we are responding to salvation, not earning it. The chapter then addresses our relationships with other believers and with those who oppose us. Romans 12:17 is therefore not a detached rule of politeness: it tests whether the Gospel is changing our reactions when we are wronged.

entries.title: Ephesians 2:1–5: From Death to Life
entries.commentary: Ephesians 2:1–5 reminds us that apart from Christ we were dead in trespasses and sins, but God, rich in mercy, gives life through Christ. This change begins with God's saving initiative, not our moral self-improvement. Compare Romans 6:1–4 and Romans 12:1–2. Genuine spiritual life bears fruit, but our fruit never purchases that life.

scriptureLinks.explanation: Saving grace brings spiritual life before the changed life that follows.

entries.title: Romans 12:14–16: The Immediate Relational Context
entries.commentary: Romans 12:14–16 calls us to bless others, share their joys and sorrows, and walk humbly together. These instructions lead naturally into verse 17. We should read its command against retaliation in the context of Paul's broader teaching about Christian relationships.

scriptureLinks.explanation: Earlier relational commands introduce the present instruction.

entries.title: Romans 12:17: Refuse Revenge; Pursue What Is Honorable
entries.commentary:
In Romans 12:17 Paul gives us two obligations: do not repay evil for evil, and take deliberate care to do what is honorable before others. Both flow from the Gospel's transforming work. We obey because we have received mercy, not because obedience earns salvation (Romans 12:1–2). Being offended never gives us permission to return the same evil.

This command does not abolish lawful justice. Exodus 21:22–25 concerns proportionate judgment in a civil setting, not a personal license to retaliate. Proverbs 20:22 and 24:29 already warn against trying to pay an offender back. We must distinguish public justice from private revenge without placing the Old and New Testaments in conflict.

Paul also requires thoughtful care in how we conduct ourselves. The Greek verb *pronoeō* (G4306), used here in Paul's instruction to respect what is right, means to consider, have regard for, or take care to. We are to consider carefully what is right and good. Compare 2 Corinthians 8:21, which concerns conduct honorable before God and others, and 1 Thessalonians 5:15, which likewise forbids returning evil for evil.

This reaches beyond outward civility. We must deal with grudges in the church, remember our witness before the world, and count the personal cost of obedience. Being wronged does not excuse us from representing Christ. We can pursue proper accountability and lawful protection without allowing revenge to govern our words, actions, or attitudes.

scriptureLinks.explanation: Transformation grounded in mercy frames the instruction to act honorably.
Proportional public justice is not authorization for private revenge.
Do not repay evil personally; trust the Lord.
Reject intent to retaliate in kind.
Deliberate honorable behavior before God and other people.
Do not return evil for evil; pursue good.
Earlier relational commands introduce the present instruction.
Jake explicitly previews three phrases but concentrates on the first in this sermon.

entries.title: Exodus 21:24: Proportional Justice, Not Private Revenge
entries.commentary: We should not appeal to “eye for eye” as permission to get even. Exodus 21:22–25 addresses the judicial treatment of wrongdoing and proportionate penalties; it does not authorize private punishment. Romans 12:17 therefore does not contradict Exodus. Proverbs 20:22 and 24:29 confirm that even the Old Testament restrains personal vengeance.

entries.title: Proverbs 20:22: Leave Retaliation with the Lord
entries.commentary: Proverbs 20:22 warns us not to promise retaliation but to trust the Lord. When we refuse to repay evil, we are not following an ethic that began only in Romans. We see the same restraint in the Old Testament, while still distinguishing private vengeance from legitimate justice.

scriptureLinks.explanation: Do not repay evil personally; trust the Lord.

entries.title: Proverbs 24:29: Reject the Payback Mindset
entries.commentary: Proverbs 24:29 exposes the temptation to say, “I will do to him as he has done to me.” We cannot justify our own wrongdoing by pointing to another person's wrongdoing. Our obligation before God is not determined by what an offender did to us.

scriptureLinks.explanation: Reject intent to retaliate in kind.

entries.title: 2 Corinthians 8:21: Integrity before Others
entries.commentary: In 2 Corinthians 8:21, Paul cares about honorable conduct before God and before other people. The immediate issue is responsible handling of a collection, but the principle helps explain Romans 12:17: we should give thoughtful attention to integrity that others can recognize, not merely claim good intentions.

scriptureLinks.explanation: Deliberate honorable behavior before God and other people.

entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 5:15: Pursue Good Instead of Payback
entries.commentary: First Thessalonians 5:15 closely parallels Romans 12:17. We must not repay evil with evil; instead, we are to pursue what is good for one another and for all. Refusing revenge is not merely staying passive. It calls us to an active pursuit of good.

scriptureLinks.explanation: Do not return evil for evil; pursue good.
